title: Linus Torvalds posts his first AI-assisted patch to the Linux kernel
content:
Linus Torvalds posts his first AI-assisted patch to the Linux kernel, synthetic test clocks 23x performance leap — the bossman makes use of AI tooling himself after issuing clear pro-AI directives
That seemingly didn't stop the pro- and against-AI camps in the kernel from continuing to bicker, though.
After a few revisions of his position on AI-assisted contributions to the Linux kernel, Linus Torvalds has posted his own first LLM-assisted patch. The development branch purports to fix an old issue with massive cache contention when many CPUs are reading the same file — a scenario potentially encountered when using shared libraries, databases, and web servers. Several developers had already made attempts over the years at fixing the issue, all with varied results, none quite ideal as an all-encompassing solution.
Torvalds posted his own draft for solving the problem in early 2024, and has used it on his own laptop since that time. However, he recently took the plunge and decided to "try to actually solve this thing using an LLM." He's now posted his solution in a development branch, and claims that he's seen a 23x performance improvement in a dedicated synthetic benchmark, though he notes that actual real-world impact will be far less significant, as "no real load" will witness those figures. If we had to guess, this improvement would benefit server workloads far more than desktop machines.
Over time, Torvalds has broadly taken a pro-AI stance on LLM tooling, at least within the purview of the tightly controlled, review-heavy environment of the Linux kernel code. Last July, he stated he's "willing to absolutely put [his] foot down" on AI haters, pointing out that an automated code review tool the kernel team uses outperforms humans, and that it caught basic programming mistakes that shouldn't have been submitted in the first place.
The team is even changing its policy to no longer require that patch authors disclose they used an AI tool when generating their code. Torvalds once again took an assertive stance, reiterating that users should treat LLMs as yet another tool, likening it to compilers or editors. In his view, he simply expects that "people do their best and [...] understand what they are doing."
Some might say that few people in the world are better-suited to properly employ an LLM than Torvalds, and by extension, kernel maintainers. There's an entire universe of difference between a senior master programmer using the LLM to speed up the boring parts of his work, and some newbie with a credit card going "claude make linux faster plz no mistakes."
However, It's not all roses. Thanks to how adept AI agents have become at recognizing common security flaw patterns, the Linux security mailing list became "unmanageable" earlier in the year. Linux has been fixing CVEs at an astonishingly rapid pace of around 2,000 per release. Still, the team's hand is being forced into dropping older hardware drivers, as they're often the target of numerous security reports, despite their negligible install base.

report.summary: Linus Torvalds submits his first LLM-assisted Linux kernel patch, claiming a 23x synthetic benchmark gain while backing AI as just another developer tool.
report.background: Linux kernel development is a massive, review-heavy open-source effort where even small changes face intense scrutiny. Torvalds has gradually shifted toward a pro-AI stance, arguing that LLMs are tools like compilers or editors and that developers must understand their work. The patch targets a long-standing cache-contention problem when many CPUs read the same file, a scenario common in shared libraries, databases, and web servers. Earlier attempts by several developers produced varied but not fully satisfactory results. Torvalds had a draft from early 2024 that he used on his laptop, then recently decided to try solving the issue with an LLM. The kernel team has also stopped requiring disclosure of AI tool use, while AI-driven security reports have stressed maintainers.
key_points: Torvalds used an LLM to help finish a patch for cache contention when many CPUs read the same file. He reports a 23x gain in a synthetic benchmark but cautions that real-world impact will be much smaller, likely benefiting server workloads more than desktop machines.

He has taken a firmly pro-AI position inside the kernel community, likening LLMs to compilers and editors and saying he expects contributors to understand what they are doing. The team no longer requires patch authors to disclose AI tool use, and Torvalds has defended automated code review that catches basic mistakes.

The kernel community remains split. Some commenters called the patch a publicity stunt or questioned how much Torvalds still codes, while others praised the approach as the right way to use AI: expert-guided, reviewed, and curated rather than blind generation.

AI has created security-side pressure too. Security agents are good at spotting common flaw patterns, making the Linux security mailing list “unmanageable,” with roughly 2,000 CVEs fixed per release. Maintainers are being forced to drop some older hardware drivers with negligible install bases because they attract many reports.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Torvalds’ patch is a high-profile validation that LLMs can assist elite developers on hard systems problems, but it also reinforces that expertise and review remain essential. For developers, it signals that AI coding is becoming normal in serious open-source work, while raising concerns about disclosure, code provenance, and deskilling. For regular users, the near-term effects are indirect: possibly faster Linux server workloads and more secure kernels, but also security triage noise and reduced support for some old hardware. The 23x figure is synthetic, not a desktop speedup.
report.tools: To follow up, read the patch discussion on lore.kernel.org and track Linux kernel releases. Try open-source or freemium coding assistants such as Continue.dev, Aider, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or Cursor, and pair them with AI code-review tools. Kernel testers can use syzkaller/syzbot for fuzzing, while security watchers should monitor Linux CVE feeds and the security mailing list.
